news.title: Max Miller stays in Ohio race as abuse allegations unsettle Republicans
news.text: Republican Congressman Max Miller is staying in the race for re-election in Ohio despite calls from within his own party to step aside over domestic abuse allegations made by his ex-wife. His decision has created difficulties for Republicans, who had not expected to spend time defending the seat in this year’s midterm elections.The contest is now increasingly being seen as competitive, with Democratic challenger Brian Poindexter using Miller’s controversies to appeal to voters by promising to “serve with honour”. Monday was the last day for Republicans to replace Miller on the general election ballot in Ohio, leaving him in the race for the 7th Congressional District.Democratic groups backing US House campaigns have been closely watching the seat, which lies south of Cleveland, to decide whether to increase support for Poindexter. President Donald Trump had won the Republican-leaning district comfortably two years ago. Miller won it with 51 per cent of the vote in a three-way contest that also included former congressman and presidential candidate Dennis Kucinich, who ran as an independent. Under Ohio’s current maps, the district leans 55 per cent to 44 per cent Republican, according to Dave’s Redistricting.Miller, 37, has said he is confident of winning because of those numbers and what he described as the goodwill he has built with constituents over two terms. Both of Ohio’s senators, including his former father-in-law Senator Bernie Moreno, had urged him to quit the race, but Trump did not. Trump called Miller “a good person” and said his legal dispute with Emily Moreno was best left for the families to sort out. Miller, who served as a senior aide to Trump during his first term, said in a CNN interview last week that the president had told him that if he stayed in, “it’s going to be a tough race”. Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters indicated the party would stand by Miller, but did not say whether it would spend money on his campaign. “We’re going to support our nominees. Everybody has to prove they are capable of winning,” Gruters said on NewsMax. “We’ll see. I hope that he can.”It was not clear on Monday whether Republican groups involved in House races, including the National Republican Campaign Committee and the Congressional Leadership Fund, would spend on Miller’s behalf. Miller said last week that he was ready to put in more of his own money. In a statement to The Wall Street Journal, which reported that he was injecting USD 1 million into the campaign, he said: “I know there are people that are concerned about my ability to win this race right now, but I don’t share that. I am invested in this election in every way, and I will invest the resources into my campaign to win.” Democratic organisations such as the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and House Majority PAC were also debating on Monday whether to make the race one of their midterm spending priorities.The race has drawn rising attention over the past month because of scrutiny over earlier abuse allegations made against Miller by his ex-wife Emily Moreno and at least two other women. Some of his efforts to defend himself have also triggered backlash. At the same time, Democrats have been encouraged by Poindexter’s chances. The 46-year-old Brook Park city councillor has campaigned on cost-of-living issues and secured endorsements from Ironworkers International, the United Auto Workers, AFSCME, the Ohio AFL-CIO and others. On Monday, he sought support from voters across the political spectrum, saying: “It’s unfortunate that Miller has chosen to keep putting his ex-wife and her family through this nightmare in the public spotlight. But let me be perfectly clear. I got into this campaign to fight for my neighbours and for working people across this district.” Miller did not respond to messages seeking comment. He was the first candidate Trump endorsed as he moved against Republicans who supported his impeachment over the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol or opposed his efforts to overturn the 2020 election result, and Miller went on to challenge Ohio Representative Anthony Gonzalez, who later dropped out. With Miller staying on the ballot, both parties are now weighing how much attention and money to devote to a race that has become far more closely watched.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 11, 2026 05:38 IST

news.title: Recount puts Trump-backed challenger in the lead of Indiana state Senate primary
news.text: A recount in a contested May Indiana state Senate primary has put Republican Paula Copenhaver, who was backed by President Donald Trump, ahead of incumbent Spencer Deery. Deery was one of seven GOP members of the Indiana state Senate who faced primary challengers this spring after voting down a redrawn congressional map that Trump pushed last year. Five lost, while Deery clung to a three-vote lead, which Copenhaver challenged. On Monday, ten votes — eight for Deery and two for Copenhaver — were thrown out by the Indiana Recount Commission over minor errors, the Indiana Capital Chronicle reported, giving Copenhaver a three-vote edge. In a post on X, Deery said he would appeal the decision. “Today, we saw members of the Indiana Recount Commission attempt to undermine the will of voters by treating ballots differently based on whether they furthered the president’s political goals,” Deery wrote. “This was not a meeting intended to find fairness; it was designed to find votes.” Copenhaver, an aide to Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. If her victory survives appeal, Copenhaver would be favored in the general election in the heavily Republican 23rd state Senate district. West Lafayette City Councilman David Sanders, a Democrat, and independent candidate Joshua Brant are also running. The new state Senate could reconsider redistricting ahead of the 2028 election. Indiana Senate President Rod Bray, who also opposed the Trump-backed map, said last month he would not seek another term as Republican leader. Trump celebrated his announcement in a Truth Social post. “I want to thank the Great State of Indiana for your support, not only in my Presidential Election, which we won with the Highest Vote in the History of the State, but also for your support in getting rid of wayward Senators, led down the Path of Destruction by a FOOL named Rodric Bray,” he wrote.
news.author: Jane C. Timm

news.title: Donald Trump Torched Over Oval Office Nap During Vaccine Update: ‘Dozing Don’
news.text:
Donald Trump found himself the butt of several jokes Monday after the president appeared to fall asleep during an update regarding childhood vaccines.

Specifically, after Trump signed an executive order Monday that reduced the number of vaccines recommended for children, as well as called for the MMR shot to be split into three separate vaccines, the president struggled to keep his eyes open as National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya spoke next to him.

It didn’t take long for the president’s apparent nap to be clipped and circulated on X, with one snippet of the snooze in-question garnering 2 million views Monday afternoon.

“Holy s–t Trump is OUT,” the X user who uploaded the clip, Aaron Rupar, wrote. Plenty of users co-signed this sentiment, with Rupar’s post nabbing 25,000 “likes.”

“‘Sleepy Joe’ [Biden] never once fell asleep like this,” another critic on X commented. “Trump does it literally all the time. Incredible.”

A third responded with, “We really need to start calling him ‘Dozing Don.’” Additionally, the X user shared a collage of all the different times the president appeared to fall asleep during official functions.

Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment.

Trump’s cognitive health has repeatedly been questioned since his inauguration in 2025, as he remains the oldest person to assume and hold the office of U.S. president.

For instance, back in June, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker once again voiced his concerns to the press about Trump’s health, alleging the president was “suffering from dementia.”

“Look at any of the videos from 2015 or 2016 and look at how he responded to questions and look at how he was at press conferences and then you fast forward and look at him now,” he told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. “I really think that there’s something genuinely wrong with him.”

Nonetheless, Trump has repeatedly denied allegations of mental deterioration, most recently claiming on Truth Social that he’s “aced” all of his cognitive tests. Trump’s June physical also defended him to be in “in excellent health, demonstrating strong cardiac, pulmonary, neurological and overall physical function.”

news.title: North Carolina GOP committee picks Jennifer Balkcom to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on November ballot
news.text: A panel of Republican officials in North Carolina selected a state lawmaker on Monday as their nominee for a House race after embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid following sexual harassment allegations. Jennifer Balkcom, who represents a state legislative district in Henderson County, will face Jamie Ager, who won the Democratic primary in March. North Carolina GOP’s Executive Committee for the 11th Congressional District picked Balkcom to replace Edwards in compliance with state law given how late in the campaign he dropped out. Edwards, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump, announced last week that he would serve out his term in Congress but would not seek a third term in the House. His decision came days after the House Ethics Committee recommended a censure following a probe that found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.” He has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, and the Ethics Committee said Edwards, who cooperated with the panel’s investigation, had denied that any of his actions were meant to be sexual or romantic in nature. Attorneys for Edwards wrote a 15-page response to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.” Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless,” and in May he said he welcomed an investigation. Edwards was elected to the House in 2022 after having ousted the scandal-ridden Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary. Before that, the district was represented by Mark Meadows, who led the House Freedom Caucus before he stepped down to become White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term. Edwards won his seat by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, but Democrats are hopeful they can flip it as Republicans seek to defend their narrow majority in the House heading into the midterm elections. Ager, a farmer who significantly outraised Edwards in the race, was previously listed as “Likely Republican” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. The rating was downgraded to “Lean Republican” before the House Ethics Committee report was released.
news.author: Raquel Coronell Uribe

news.title: US-Iran war LIVE: Oil prices extend gains for third day as Trump lashes out at Iran, makes new demands
news.text: US-Iran War LIVE: Oil prices on Monday held a three-day gain after US President Donald Trump made sweeping new demands on Iran, clouding the outlook for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate traded near $82 a barrel after closing 5.1% higher in the previous session, while Brent settled below $88. The developments came after Iran and Oman had been negotiating a deal to reopen the strategic waterway. However, Tehran on Monday reiterated that any accord would require Washington to end the naval blockade and compensate Iran for damages. Before the war, roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas was shipped through the Strait of Hormuz to global markets.Trump makes sweeping new demands, lashes out at IranThe US President lashed out at Iran on Monday (local time) and made sweeping new demands, including compensation from the Islamic Republic for all the people it has killed in conflicts, after Tehran reiterated requests for reparations as part of talks to wind down the conflict. In a Truth Social post, he said the new demands will be put “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations.” He also said that compensation for Iran “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings.” But a 14-point memorandum of understanding that Tehran and Washington agreed to in June detailed plans for the US and regional partners to develop a $300 billion fund for the “rehabilitation and economic development” of Iran after the war.Trump reiterates Strait of Hormuz is open nowOn Monday, Trump, when asked what's next for Iran after the Islamic Republic rejected Washington's demands, told ABC News, "You'll find out." Commenting on whether escalation is still on the table, he added, "Well, we have that -- certainly that ability if we want to do that. Yeah, you'll find out." The US President once again reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz is now open and completely controlled by Washington, but acknowledged that Tehran could “make trouble.”Iran accuses US of being "incapable" of pursuing diplomacyIranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei on Tuesday criticised the Trump administration over its sanctions policy, accusing Washington of being "addicted" to economic restrictions after US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent reportedly claimed that sanctions were "suffocating" Iran. In a post on X, Baqaei said the repeated use of sanctions reflected the United States' inability to pursue diplomacy. He wrote, "The US Secretary of the Treasury has boasted of 'suffocating' Iran through economic sanctions. Beyond its sheer pathos, the claim is a stark testament to America's compulsive addiction to sanctions." The Iranian official further alleged that whenever Washington fails to achieve its objectives via diplomacy, it turns to sanctions and increases their intensity when they do not yield results.

news.title: US revokes 175,000 visas since Trump's 2nd term began
news.text:
The U.S. State Department on Monday announced that it has revoked more than 175,000 visas since January 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term, reported Xinhua.

 "The majority of these visas were revoked due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity, with assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes being the leading causes," the department said in a statement.

 "A significant share of visas were revoked for reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement, and other crimes," the statement said.

 "A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right. The Department remains committed to using every tool available to protect our communities from those who abuse it," the statement added.

 Since Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders.

news.title: Iran says service fees should be charged for passage through Hormuz
news.text:
Fees should be charged for maritime services provided in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday, reported Xinhua.

 He made the remarks at a weekly press conference in response to a question about whether fees for maritime services had been discussed during negotiations between Iran and Oman on the designation of a new route in the waterway.

 "Generally, when you provide maritime services, you must be reimbursed for them," Baghaei said.

 "At this stage, we do not discuss such details," he said, adding that the discussions were continuing and "certain technical points" will be discussed.

 Baghaei said the negotiations between Iran and Oman "are being held smoothly and constructively," noting that mechanisms would be established to ensure safe shipping, address environmental issues, provide maritime services and combat crimes in the strait.

 Under a potential agreement to be reached between the two sides, the existing northern and southern routes in the strait would be replaced by an intermediate one, he said, adding that the new route would be used temporarily until Iran and Oman agree on a new traffic separation scheme.

 Baghaei attributed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to U.S. and Israeli "military aggression" against Iran, saying its reopening hinges on the elimination of the conditions imposed on Iran.

 He repeated that Iran is not negotiating with the United States, but the two countries continue to exchange messages through mediators. 

 Iran tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 28 following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian territory.

 On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding on ending the war. Under the deal, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days to reach a final agreement, but the future of the talks has become uncertain following an escalation between the two sides last month.

Trump wants compensation from Iran as Tehran seeks war damages

US President Donald Trump on Monday rejected Iran's demand for financial compensation over damages incurred during the US-Israeli military operations in the country, asserting that Tehran must instead be held accountable for casualties resulting from its own actions, reported ANI.

Taking to Truth Social, the US President noted that Iranian representatives were seeking compensation for damage caused during the "last five months Military Conflict", which he stated erupted after Iran refused to give up its nuclear weapons ambition.

Describing Iran's demand for compensation as an "interesting idea", Trump indicated that he would present a counter-demand during future diplomatic negotiations.

The US President stated that Tehran must face claims for financial restitution over casualties and injuries caused by attacks linked to Iran, including the 2000 USS Cole bombing and several other regional incidents.

"I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded," Trump posted on Truth Social.

Trump made specific reference to Iran's late military commander Qassem Soleimani, alleging that Tehran's leadership was involved in conflicts that led to thousands of fatalities. Soleimani was killed in a targeted drone strike authorised by Trump in 2020 in Baghdad, Iraq.

Extending the scope of his counter-claim, Trump also demanded compensation for the families of protesters who, he alleged, were killed by the Iranian regime over the past five decades. He further claimed that 52,000 people had lost their lives over the course of the last five months.

Confirming his stance, the US President stated that he has instructed American negotiators to integrate these conditions into all upcoming diplomatic talks with Tehran.

"I have instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any, and all, future negotiations," Trump wrote.

The counter-demand follows Tehran linking war reparation claims to conditions for a possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, alongside the lifting of US sanctions and the end of naval blockades.

Iran's ability to disrupt commercial shipping through the strategically important waterway has constrained American strategic options, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.

The report noted that sporadic missile and drone attacks have severely impacted commercial maritime traffic while triggering mounting concerns across global markets.

Although US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the maritime corridor was open, commercial shipping activity across the region remained heavily disrupted. 

Trump also issued warnings of a "massive bombing campaign" against Tehran, though the report indicated that Iranian authorities appeared prepared for an extended conflict.

Underscoring Tehran's firm stance, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) stated on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until Washington agreed to all of Tehran's conditions, including financial restitution for war damage.

The statement followed earlier remarks by Iranian security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who called for an end to the "war and aggression" against Iran alongside its regional allies across Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq.

Reiterating its position, the Guards declared that the maritime transit route would continue to serve as a "theatre of war" until the US met all of Iran's stipulations in full.

news.title: Trump extends Jones Act waiver 90 days for foreign ships moving energy, fertilizers
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) - President Donald Trump on Monday extended a waiver for 90 days for foreign ships to transport goods, including oil, fertilizers and other fossil fuel products, among U.S. ports.

The president first waived the Jones Act on March 17 so that it would be easier to transport oil and refined fuels among ports, reducing price pressures after the start of the war with Iran.

The latest extension will take effect on August 17 and suggests that the U.S. might be preparing for continued price pressures as the Strait of Hormuz, a primary waterway for shipping oil and natural gas, remains effectively closed because of the war.

Unlike previous extensions, the Pentagon will consult with the Maritime Administration to decide which voyages are exempt from the 1920 law containing the Jones Act. The new waiver will only apply to cargo that are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture such as fertilizers and soybean oil.

news.title: Trump signs order calling for spacing out of childhood jabs
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order calling for a shake-up of childhood immunisation guidelines that back his controversial theories that jabs for children should be spaced out into separate medical visits.

The order calls for separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots administered in separate visits, and directs the US health department to improve vaccine research, says a White House fact sheet.

Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for children are not currently available in the United States.

During the signing of the order in the Oval Office, Trump described the move as “another historic step to make America healthy again”.

The president also suggested the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder, despite scientific consensus and decades of studies finding there is no connection.

The renewed focus on vaccines marks a departure from his administration’s recent efforts to emphasise less controversial health policies ahead of November’s midterm elections, reports The Associated Press.

Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.

Childhood vaccines - and how and when to give them in combination - go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.

Trump called the announcement a “major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science.”

But Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said the announcement spreads uncertainty, fear and confusion where “there doesn’t need to be any of that.” 

He disputed the Trump administration’s recommendations and said previous ones should stand.

“Science about vaccines and their efficacy has not changed,” he said.

“The distribution of viruses and other pathogens in our environment has not changed. Children in this country have not changed in the last 48 hours.”

Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.

“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” he wrote. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes.”

The executive order signed on Monday comes after other vaccine actions by the Trump administration.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before he entered politics, set out to overhaul immunisation guidance at the Department of Health Services in the first year of Trump’s term.

He fired an entire 17-member vaccine advisory committee, installing replacements who made far more restrictive recommendations that have since been halted by a federal judge.
news.author: Richard Wood

news.title: Trump's Secret Plane Switch: How Iran Assassination Threat Triggered Air Force One Decoy
news.text: US President Donald Trump secretly switched from Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft while leaving Turkey last month after an Iranian assassination threat, according to an investigation by The Washington Post. The extraordinary operation meant journalists and some White House staff travelling on the Presidential aircraft believed Trump was aboard, while he was actually flown separately to Britain, the newspaper reported. The operation took place on July 8, shortly after US forces resumed strikes on Iran following the collapse of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end their months-long war. A US official familiar with the operation and another person with knowledge of Trump's travel told the Post that the operation was prompted by a "credible threat" against the President. Inside Trump's Secret Move Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard the newer Boeing 747-8 aircraft gifted to the US by Qatar. He had announced that he would leave Turkey aboard the older blue-and-white Boeing 747 that had previously served as Air Force One, rather than the Qatari aircraft. Television cameras filmed Trump boarding the legacy Air Force One at Ankara airport. But, according to the Post, he was secretly transferred minutes later to a smaller US Air Force C-32A. The transfer was carried out using an airport catering truck normally used to load food and other supplies onto aircraft, according to the newspaper's sources and material it reviewed. The operation turned the legacy Air Force One into a "decoy", with journalists and some White House staff aboard while Trump was on the C-32A, one US official told the Post. The C-32A had been flown to Turkey alongside the two Boeing 747s to support the President's visit. It is a modified Boeing 757 normally used to transport senior US government officials and can also carry the President or vice-President. The operation meant that Trump's actual location was concealed from the public and some senior officials for several hours. As journalists boarded the legacy Air Force One, White House staff instructed them to close the aircraft's window shades, according to a media pool report. The Post said footage from Ankara showed a catering truck positioned beside the legacy Air Force One, with its container raised to the level of the aircraft. Trump arrived in a limousine, climbed the aircraft's stairs and waved towards the tarmac before boarding. Minutes later, according to the newspaper, the catering truck moved away from Air Force One and towards the C-32A. A man in a suit was seen entering the truck's cab, while the container was lowered before the vehicle drove towards the smaller aircraft. The Post said the footage appeared to show a person later climbing the stairs into the C-32A. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the smaller aircraft separately using external stairs, according to the newspaper's sources and other material it reviewed. Hegseth travelled with Trump to Britain on the C-32A, the Post reported. Iran Threat Prompted Operation The operation came amid heightened concerns about threats against Trump from Iran. US intelligence officials had previously flagged a specific threat of an attack against the President or his aircraft, according to reports by The New York Times and CBS News. The US has long been concerned about Iranian plots targeting American officials. Those concerns have intensified following US involvement in the killing of senior Iranian military and political figures. In response to questions from the Post, White House communications director Steven Cheung defended the security of the aircraft gifted by Qatar. "The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff," Cheung said. "As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats." Publicly available flight-tracking data reviewed by the Post suggests that the three aircraft followed different paths after leaving Turkey. The Qatari aircraft flew to RAF Mildenhall in Britain using the call sign "SAM 33". The legacy Air Force One, carrying journalists and White House staff, later appeared on radar near Istanbul and eventually adopted the "AF1" call sign despite Trump not being aboard. It arrived at Mildenhall at about 22:29 local time, according to the data. The C-32A did not appear in publicly available flight-tracking data, but videos posted online showed the aircraft arriving in Britain at about 22:20, followed by the legacy Air Force One several minutes later. During the flight back to the US, Trump spoke to journalists for about 15 minutes. He discussed the threat posed by Iran but did not publicly acknowledge the aircraft switch. Asked why reporters had been instructed to lower the window shades while in Turkey, Mr Trump said: "because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with." He said he faced a threat to his life "all the time" and claimed he was "number one" on Iran's "list". "But if I go, you go. Right?" Trump told reporters. "Perhaps someday you want to change professions." The revelation comes amid continuing scrutiny of the newer aircraft gifted to the US by Qatar. The aircraft has been criticised over the extent of its defensive capabilities compared with the legacy Presidential jets. The Trump administration has defended its security. "The aircraft is safe, secure, and equipped with the most advanced technologies necessary to meet requirements of the Presidential mission," the US Air Force said in a statement. "No risk was taken in security, safety, or mission communications," it added.
news.summary: Concerns about threats to Trump had escalated amid US-Iran tensions, prompting heightened security measures during his travels.
news.author: Rounak Bagchi

news.title: Deadline passes for Rep. Max Miller to be replaced on Ohio ballot as he faces domestic abuse claims
news.text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller is staying in the race for his Ohio congressional district, defying voices within his own party who urged him to step aside as he faced domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife.

His determination to press on with his reelection campaign is creating headaches for a Republican Party that had not planned to devote attention to defending the seat in this year’s midterm elections. His Democratic challenger, union ironworker Brian Poindexter, seized on Miller’s controversies by appealing to voters with a promise to “serve with honor.”

Monday presented the last chance for Republicans to replace Miller on the general election ballot in Ohio, leaving the congressman in what is increasingly seen as a competitive race.

Democratic groups supporting U.S. House campaigns have been closely watching the race for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, just south of Cleveland, to see if they want to ramp up their support for Poindexter.

President Donald Trump won the GOP-leaning district comfortably two years ago. Miller won it with just 51% of the vote two years ago in a three-way contest that included former congressman and presidential candidate Dennis Kucinich, who ran as an independent. Under Ohio’s current maps, the district leans 55%-44% Republican, according to Dave’s Redistricting.

Miller, 37, has said he is confident he can pull out a win, given those odds and the goodwill he said he has built with constituents over his two terms. While both of Ohio’s senators, including his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno, called on him to drop out of the race, Trump never did.

The Republican president called Miller “a good person” and said his legal dispute with Emily Moreno is best left to the families to figure out. Miller was a senior aide to Trump during his first term as president.

In a CNN interview last week, Miller said the president told him that if he stayed in, “it’s going to be a tough race.” Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters suggested the party would back Miller but stopped short of saying it would spend on his campaign.

“We’re going to support our nominees. Everybody has to prove they are capable of winning,” Gruters said during a Sunday appearance on NewsMax. “We’ll see. I hope that he can.”

It was unclear Monday if Republican groups invested in House races, such as the National Republican Campaign Committee or the super PAC Congressional Leadership Fund, would spend on Miller’s behalf.

Miller last week said he was prepared to spend more of his own money on his campaign.

“I know there are people that are concerned about my ability to win this race right now, but I don’t share that,” Miller said in a statement to The Wall Street Journal for a report on him infusing $1 million of his own money into the campaign. “I am invested in this election in every way, and I will invest the resources into my campaign to win.”

Democratic groups such as the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and House Majority PAC were debating Monday whether to include the race among their midterm spending priorities

The race has been drawing increasing attention over the past month amid scrutiny of previous abuse allegations made against Miller by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and at least two other women. Some of his attempts to defend himself also have drawn backlash.

At the same time, Democrats have been heartened by Poindexter’s prospects. The 46-year-old Brook Park city councilman has campaigned on pocketbook issues and won union endorsements from the Ironworkers International, United Auto Workers, AFSCME, Ohio AFL-CIO and others.

Poindexter on Monday sought to capitalize on Miller’s controversies by welcoming voters across the political spectrum to support his campaign.

“It’s unfortunate that Miller has chosen to keep putting his ex-wife and her family through this nightmare in the public spotlight,” he said in a statement. “But let me be perfectly clear. I got into this campaign to fight for my neighbors and for working people across this district.”

Miller did not return messages seeking comment.

Miller was the first person Trump endorsed as he sought to punish fellow Republicans who voted in favor of his impeachment over the Jan. 6, 2021, violent assault on the U.S. Capitol or blocked his efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election, which was won by Democrat Joe Biden. The then-32-year-old jumped in to challenge Ohio Rep. Anthony Gonzalez, a popular former professional football player, who ultimately dropped out.

Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa.
news.author: Julie Carr Smyth And Thomas Beaumont The Associated Press

news.title: Todd Blanche Sworn In as Attorney General in Oval Office Ceremony
news.text:
Todd Blanche, President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer, was sworn in Monday as U.S. attorney general and now formally takes the helm of the Justice Department.

Judge Emil Bove, a federal appeals court judge and former member of Trump’s legal defense team, administered the oath in a closed Oval Office ceremony that the president attended. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt later shared a video of the event.

The 50–49 vote took place shortly after 4 a.m.

Two Republicans, Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, sided with Democrats in voting no. Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, still recovering from health issues, was absent.

Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana gave the decisive yes vote. The Louisiana Republican, who had expressed doubts about the department’s direction, told colleagues Friday that Blanche represented a sensible appointment under the current administration.

“The choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche,” Cassidy said on the Senate floor. “It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump, and who indeed may not be as good as Mr. Blanche.”

Murkowski pointed to decisions she believed suggested insufficient independence. Collins said Blanche is a capable lawyer but remained conflicted over the apparent politicization of the Justice Department.

Blanche posted a statement thanking the Senate.

“I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General,” he wrote. “I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process.”

After the vote, senators left Washington for a five-week recess.
news.author: Kimberly Hayek
